findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted condition and wrong offset, so it never validates the grant shortcut
findings.body: In AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId (line 483), the check `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` is inverted: it returns false (no match) exactly when the extracted characters EQUAL the expected grant shortcut, and continues (match) when they differ. Additionally, the offset is wrong: in the encoded token ID the grant-type shortcut occupies characters at indices 4-5 (after 2 chars of session type and 2 chars of token type), so it should be `substring(4, 6)`; `substring(3, 5)` reads the second token-type char plus the first grant char. Net effect: for a correctly encoded ID like `onrtac:<uuid>`, the matcher extracts "ta", which never equals "ac", so the grant shortcut is effectively not checked at all — tests using expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken would pass even if the server encoded the wrong grant type, and could spuriously fail for IDs whose characters 3-4 coincidentally equal the expected shortcut. Fix both the negation and the substring bounds.

findings.title: Constructor null-checks grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId
findings.body: In AccessTokenContext's constructor, line 73 reads `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` — a copy/paste of the grantType check on line 72. The `rawTokenId` parameter is therefore never null-checked: a null rawTokenId is silently accepted, and if it ever triggered, the exception message would misleadingly say "Null grantType not allowed". Change the second check to `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

findings.title: New abstract getShortcut() method breaks existing third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations
findings.body: Adding `String getShortcut();` as an abstract method to the public SPI interface OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a source- and binary-incompatible change: every existing custom grant-type factory deployed as an extension will fail to compile against the new version, and pre-built jars will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when Keycloak's DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory calls getShortcut() during postInit (which happens at server startup, so the whole server can fail to boot for those deployments). Provide a `default` implementation (e.g. deriving a shortcut from getId() or returning a documented fallback) to preserve compatibility.

findings.title: Public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context) removed and grantType becomes stale after setFormParams
findings.body: Two related issues in OAuth2GrantType.Context: (1) The public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` was deleted. It was part of the public SPI surface (this class lives in server-spi-private and is implemented/used by third-party grant extensions), so removing it is a compile-time break for any external code that wrapped or derived a Context. (2) The new `grantType` field is captured once in the constructor from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`, but `setFormParams(...)` (which external grant implementations can use to swap in re-parsed form params) does not refresh `grantType`. Consequently, when token issuance later reads `context.getGrantType()` in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse and encodes it into the access-token ID, the encoded grant type can be wrong/stale relative to the form params actually in effect, silently corrupting the context metadata this PR introduces.

findings.title: Lazy map refresh can silently corrupt grant-type/shortcut mappings on shortcut collisions
findings.body: In getShortcutByGrantType (and getGrantTypeByShortcut), when a grant type is not found in the cached maps, the factory refreshes the cache by blindly doing `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` without checking whether that shortcut is already mapped to a different grant type. If a newly deployed custom grant reuses a shortcut already assigned to another grant (e.g. "ac"), the put overwrites the existing reverse mapping, and from then on tokens containing that shortcut decode to the wrong grant type — data corruption in the token context with no warning. Note the duplicate-shortcut validation only runs once in postInit (line 82), so dynamically deployed/hot-reloaded grants bypass it entirely. The lazy refresh path should detect the collision (existing mapping to a different grant) and fail loudly (log error / throw) instead of overwriting, mirroring the postInit validation.

findings.title: Lightweight-token detection reads the session-context client rather than the client the token is issued for
findings.body: getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext determines the token type via AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session), which evaluates `session.getContext().getClient().getAttribute(USE_LIGHTWEIGHT_ACCESS_TOKEN_ENABLED)`. TokenManager.initToken receives the issuing `client` as a parameter, but this path relies on the ambient session-context client being set to the same client; where they diverge (or where the session-context client is null, e.g. token creation invoked from non-request contexts such as backchannel flows or tests), the lookup either returns the wrong client's lightweight setting or throws an NPE. The client used for the lightweight check should be taken from the client session / passed explicitly rather than from session.getContext().

findings.title: Unit test bypasses factory postInit, so real grant-shortcut wiring is untested
findings.body: The test's before() method hand-injects a synthetic map (only 'ro', 'cc' and 'na') into the package-private fields instead of running DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit with a real KeycloakSessionFactory, and passes a null session to the provider. As a result, the code paths that production actually exercises — populating maps from the real OAuth2GrantType factories, the postInit duplicate-shortcut validation, and the lazy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut (which dereferences sessionFactory and would NPE in these tests if hit) — have no coverage. There is also no end-to-end/integration test asserting that issued access tokens actually carry the expected prefix (e.g. an authorization-code login produces `on..ac:`), which is the main behavior of this PR; the only integration-level check (AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId) is itself buggy (see separate finding).
